items.title: Agencies Announce Dollar Thresholds for Applicability of Truth in Lending and Consumer Leasing Rules for Consumer Credit and Lease Transactions
items.content_text:
The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing).
By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations.
Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.
Read the Consumer Leasing (Regulation M)
Read the Truth in Lending (Regulation Z)

items.title: Federal Financial Participation in State Assistance Expenditures; Federal Matching Shares for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, and Aid to Needy Aged, Blind, or Disabled Persons for October 1, 2027, Through September 30, 2028
items.content_text: The Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (FMAP) and Enhanced Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (eFMAP) for fiscal year 2028 have been calculated pursuant to the Social Security Act (the Act). These percentages will be effective from October 1, 2027, through September 30, 2028. This notice announces the calculated FMAP rates, in accordance with the Act, that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will use in determining the amount of Federal matching for State medical assistance (Medicaid), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Contingency Funds, Child Support collections, Child Care Mandatory and Matching Funds of the Child Care and Development Fund, Title IV-E Foster Care Maintenance payments, Adoption Assistance payments and Kinship Guardianship Assistance payments, and the eFMAP rates for the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) expenditures. Table 1 gives figures for each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. This notice reminds states of adjustments available for states meeting requirements for disproportionate employer pension or insurance fund contributions and adjustments for disaster recovery. At this time, no state qualifies for such adjustments, and territories are not eligible.

items.title: Standing Order: Standing Order Requiring Paper Filing for Election Day 2026 Emergency Matters
items.content_text:
STATE OF MAINE       SUPERIOR COURT 
DISTRICT COURT 
 
  
STANDING ORDER REQUIRING 
PAPER FILING FOR ELECTION DAY 
2026 EMERGENCY MATTERS 
 
 
 The Maine Judicial Branch (MJB) is implementing the Maine eCourts 
system – including eFiling – statewide.1  EFileMaine is a practical and efficient 
document submission system already in use in many courts throughout the 
state.  However, because filings related to Election Day may be uniquely time-
sensitive, to ensure timely processing, the MJB will require paper filing under 
the limited circumstances described below.   
 
 It is therefore ORDERED that any emergency Title 21-A filings related to 
Election Day 2026 filed between 4:00 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, and 
9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, must be by paper, unless otherwise 
ordered.2 
 
It is further ORDERED that the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems 
are SUSPENDED to the extent necessary to give effect to this order.   
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   _____/s/______________________   
       Chief Justice Robert E. Mullen 
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   ___/s/_______________________   
       Chief Judge Brent Davis 
 
1 Further information about the Maine eCourts system is available at 
https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html 
2 Any Election Day 2026 filings filed by eFile during this period may not be processed until the next business 
day after the election.

Title IV PostsecondaryInstitutions: Workforce Pell Program Applications Open for Second Review Cycle Through Nov. 13

October 14, 2026

For Immediate Release

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist | media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA -The State Workforce Development Board(SWDB) is accepting applications from Title IV postsecondary institutionsseeking stateapproval to offer programs eligible for federal Workforce Pell Grants. Applications for the second review cycle are due Friday, Nov. 13

Maine's Workforce Pell application provides an online process for eligible postsecondary institutions to seek approval to offer short-term workforce training programs that meet federal Workforce Pell Grant requirements. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis and reviewed quarterly by the SWDB.

Workforce Pell expands federal Pell Grant eligibility to approved short-term workforce training programs that prepare students for high-skill, high-wage and in-demand careers. States are responsible for reviewing and certifying eligible programs before they are submitted to the U.S. Department of Education for final approval.

"Workforce Pell opens the door to new education and career opportunities for more people across our state,"said Vaughan Woodruff, chair of the State Workforce Development Board."The program's support for training that connects people with skills needed for Maine's workforce presents a significant opportunity for Maine workers and employers."

The Maine Workforce Pell Program Determination Policy establishesthe state's process foridentifying, reviewing and recommending eligible short-term workforce training programs for Workforce Pell. The policy was developed in partnership with the Maine Department of Labor, Maine Department of Education, Finance Authority of Maine, Maine Community College System and University of MaineSystem.

"Workforce Pell brings a new source of federal funding to Maine's short-term workforce training programs," said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. "We are excited to help Maine's postsecondary institutions take advantage of this opportunity to strengthen their programs, reach more students and prepare Maine's workforce for the future."

The SWDB will evaluate applications and make recommendations to the Governor for state certification. Programs certified by the Governor will then be submitted to the U.S. Department of Education for final approval. Following federal approval, the SWDB will publish the list of Maine-certified Workforce Pell programs on the Maine Workforce Pell webpage within 30 days.

Institutions can find the Workforce Pell application, eligibility requirements, program guidance and additional information on the Maine Workforce Pell webpage.

125  BUREAU OF REVENUE SERVICES

Chapter 806: NONRESIDENT INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: This rule provides income tax guidance for nonresident individuals in the 
following areas: 
 
• Determination of Maine-source income; 
• Deduction of Maine losses; 
• Attribution and apportionment of income, tax additions and tax credits to Maine; 
• Returns, worksheets and schedules to be used for filing; 
• Determination of taxable income and tax credits for spouses filing as single 
individuals; and 
• Income tax withholding obligations.

.03 Income not subject to Maine income tax 
.04 Deduction of losses 
.05 Special sourcing rules 
.06 Income tax credits 
.07 Return of nonresident or part-year resident individual 
.08 Maine taxable income computation for spouses filing as single individuals 
.09 Maine tax additions and tax credits for spouses filing as single individuals 
.10 Maine income tax withholding obligations 
.11 Application date 
 
 
 
 
.01 Definitions.  As used in this rule, unless the context otherwise indicates or may otherwise 
require, the following terms have the following meanings that shall apply throughout the 
rule. 
 
A. Code.   “Code” means the United States Internal Revenue Code of 1986 and 
amendments to that Code as of the date stated in 36 M.R.S. § 111(1-A).

its old law on carry permits with new laws that achieved a similar result.

The Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 
(RLUIPA) was enacted pursuant to Congress's Spending Clause author-

prison systems like the Louisiana Department of Corrections (LDOC).

ligious exercises. See 42 U. S. C. §§ 2000cc–1(a), (b)(1). Relying on 
that provision, inmate Damon Landor brought this RLUIPA lawsuit

30 OCTOBER TERM, 2025 
Syllabus 
PUNG, PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE OF THE 
ESTATE OF PUNG v. ISABELLA COUNTY, 
MICHIGAN 
certiorari to the united states court of appeals for 
the sixth circuit 
No. 25–95. Argued February 25, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 
The Pung family owed $2,241.93 in real-property taxes, so local tax author-
ities in Isabella County, Michigan, initiated foreclosure proceedings and 
sold the Pung home—which was assessed at $194,400 for tax purposes— 
for $76,008 at public auction. Michael Pung sued in Federal court, and 
the District Court granted Pung partial summary judgment on his Fifth 
Amendment claim. The court held that Pung should receive only the 
surplus proceeds from the tax sale—i. e., the difference between the 
sale price and the tax debt—not the property's fair market value. The 
District Court also rejected Pung's claim under the Eighth Amendment 
Excessive Fines Clause. The Sixth Circuit affrmed. 
Held: 
1. The proper baseline for measuring “just compensation” following a 
tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property's hypothetical fair 
market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the 
country's history of tax sales. Pp. 35–43. 
(a) For hundreds of years, English and American law have allowed 
the seizure and sale of property as a tax-collection method, provided 
that the government return any surplus proceeds to the debtor. Fed-
eral statutes from the early days of the Republic applied this rule,

Maine's Minimum Wage to Increase to $15.70 Per Hour in 2027

September 18, 2026

For Immediate Release: September 18, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor announced today that, effective January 1, 2027, the state minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 per hour, based on data recently made available by the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. MDOL is required under Maine law (Maine statute Title 26, chapter 7, section 664) to make annual adjustments to the minimum wage based on the cost-of-living index (CPI-W) for the Northeast Region, after Maine voters amended the law by referendum in 2016. Between August 2025 and August 2026, there was a 4.1 percent increase in the CPI-W.

According to the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey for 2025, there were 28,000 hourly workers who were paid less than $15.00 per hour. These workers represent about four percent of all wage and salary workers (both paid at hourly rates and not paid at hourly rates) and about eight percent of wage and salary workers who are paid at hourly rates.

Agricultural workers in Maine are also entitled to the state minimum wage, after the Legislature enacted and Governor Mills signed "An Act to Establish a State Minimum Hourly Wage for Agricultural Workers" in 2025.

The "tip wage," or service employee minimum wage, will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour. This means that service employees must receive a direct cash wage of at least $7.85 per hour from the employer. The employer must be able to show that the employee receives at least the minimum wage of $15.70 per hour when the direct wage and tips are combined at the end of the week. The amount of tips necessary to qualify as a service employee will increase from $191 to $199 per month.

The minimum salary threshold for exempting a worker from overtime pay must exceed 3,000 times the State's minimum wage or the annualized rate established by the U.S. Department of Labor, whichever is higher. Starting January 1, 2027, the new minimum salary threshold for salaried workers exempt from overtime will be $905.79 per week, or $47,101.08 per year. This is only one of the factors used in determining whether a worker is exempt from overtime pay under federal or state law. An individual can earn more than the minimum salary threshold and still be eligible for overtime. The duties of each worker must be considered as part of this analysis.

Employers can download the required minimum wage poster at no cost on the Department's website.

The minimum wage and overtime law can be found here.

More information about minimum wage and other labor standards is available on the Department's website

STATE OF MAINE 
 
v. 
 
HEATHER MARICHAL

No. 24–1234. Argued March 2, 2026—Decided June 18, 2026

born in Texas. He has spent most of his life living in the Dallas area 
with his parents and working a stable job. Suspecting Mr. Hemani and 
his family members of terrorism-related activities, the government con-
ducted a search of the family home in 2022. Throughout the process, 
Mr. Hemani proved cooperative: he surrendered a gun he kept in the 
house, pointed agents to some marijuana on the property, and consented 
to an interview during which he told law enforcement agents that he 
used marijuana about every other day. More than six months after the

arguing that the government's effort to enforce § 922(g)(3) against him 
violated the Second Amendment. The district court granted the mo-
tion, and after an unsuccessful appeal to the Fifth Circuit, the govern-
ment asked this Court to review the case.
